scope: inventory.json groups.tooling: tooling, config, docs, acceptance and historical provenance
review_mode: Read-only implementation review; only this requested report is written. No suite execution, dependency installation, service startup or code modification.
verdict: Changes requested for lifecycle reliability, truthful gate evidence and seed atomicity; additional guard coverage findings included.

findings.title: Container ownership is recorded only after allocation, so failed creation can escape every cleanup path
findings.evidence: Dependency and compatibility launchers capture stdout and register an ID only after create returns successfully with a valid ID. Timeout or nonzero/malformed output after allocation leaves no recorded cleanup authority. Compatibility has no recovery name or cidfile at all. OCI run similarly appends only after check_output succeeds, and the browser is launched by podman run --rm without durable ownership. Killing/timing out a Podman client is not proof its container was never allocated or stopped. The dependency launcher explicitly reports uncertainty but its caller subsequently runs down and can erase the remaining state file.
findings.consequence: Interrupted or partially successful acceptance leaves orphaned containers/volumes and occupied fixed ports, while the surviving manifest can incorrectly look fully cleaned. Subsequent runs cannot safely identify these resources.
findings.remedy: Consolidate disposable-container creation/removal into one narrow owner used by dependencies, compatibility, OCI and browser gates. Persist provisional creation obligations and unique cidfile paths before spawning; recover and validate exact IDs even on failure; retain unresolved evidence when allocation is unknown. Never infer removal authority from a name or prune. Keep one canonical fixture/image configuration rather than maintaining separate launcher definitions.
findings.verification: Add launcher-level fault tests for create timeout before/after cidfile publication, malformed/nonzero output after allocation, failed start, browser timeout and interruption. Assert every known exact ID is removed, unresolved allocation remains explicitly recorded, and unrelated containers/volumes are untouched. Then have the verification owner run real isolated lifecycle acceptance.
findings.validation_status: Source-traced; no fault probes or suites executed in this read-only review.

findings.title: Cleanup aborts at the first failure and the verifier does not handle SIGTERM
findings.evidence: The native finally block raises immediately after killing the first process that exceeds its deadline; later processes are not waited/reaped. OCI stop/rm and dependency down use check=True inside loops, so one failure prevents attempts on remaining IDs. verify.py registers no SIGTERM handler, unlike dev.py, so ordinary termination does not enter its finally blocks. Existing dev_lifecycle exercises only dev.py after readiness, not verifier interruption, startup interruption or cleanup failure.
findings.consequence: One unhealthy child/Podman removal or CI termination can strand the rest of the owned run. The advertised lifecycle guarantee is supported only on the normal cleanup path. Cleanup errors can also mask the original failing gate.
findings.remedy: Use a shared bounded process/resource owner that attempts all registered cleanups, kills and reaps every surviving child, retains failed resource IDs, and reports aggregate cleanup errors after preserving the primary failure. Install INT/TERM handling at the verifier composition root and manage subprocess groups where grandchildren exist. Keep cancellation and cleanup behavior identical across dev, verify and compatibility rather than maintaining separate loops.
findings.verification: Inject a first-child shutdown timeout and a first-container stop/remove failure with additional resources registered; require later cleanup still happens. Send SIGTERM to the verifier during dependency creation, browser execution and native operation; assert bounded exit, no owned processes/known containers left, and retained uncertain IDs.
findings.validation_status: Source-traced; execution reserved for separate verification owner.

findings.title: Failed or interrupted gates can leave an apparently successful evidence ledger
findings.evidence: run() writes output/results only after subprocess.run returns normally. TimeoutExpired, spawn failure and interruption record neither that failing gate nor captured partial output. results.json is not initialized at run start; an early failure can leave the prior complete success ledger. Assertions such as generation drift and final cleanup are outside the recorded gates, so a nonzero verifier can still leave only exit_code=0 entries. The acceptance ledger calls results.json the final gate authority.
findings.consequence: Maintainers cannot distinguish a completed successful run from a partial/failed run by consuming the published evidence file; the most useful timeout diagnostics are lost and older logs can be mistaken for current output.
findings.remedy: Initialize a run-scoped ledger with revision, run identifier, start time, expected gates and running status before side effects. Record each gate as started then completed/failed/timed-out/interrupted in a finally-safe path, preserving partial output. Record generation-drift and cleanup failures and atomically publish an overall completed status only after all gates and cleanup finish. Keep historical evidence separate from the current run rather than overwriting mixed snapshots.
findings.verification: With a prior green ledger present, exercise a first-gate spawn failure, timeout with partial stdout, generation mismatch, later assertion and cleanup failure. Each must produce a current failed/incomplete run with its cause, never a stale successful ledger; a successful run must have all expected gates and cleanup completed.
findings.validation_status: Source-traced. Frozen results were independently parsed as 25 zero-exit historical gates and 39 Rust passes; this is not current execution evidence.

findings.title: Seed identity conflicts are checked after committing ownership mutations
findings.evidence: The fixture ignores a collision on the fixed user ID, then grants that ID owner memberships and inserts tenant/project rows, and COMMITs. Only a separate connection checks whether that ID actually has owner@example.test. If the ID already belongs to a different mailbox, the script raises after granting the conflicting identity ownership of the fixture tenants. Organization/project ID collisions are also silently retained; the count query does not validate their exact shape.
findings.consequence: The documented conflict-fails-without-overwriting-ownership behavior is not atomic: a failed seed can leave committed incorrect ownership and partial fixture effects. Even though this is restricted to disposable development data, rerun/conflict safety is an explicit onboarding contract.
findings.remedy: Validate all fixed fixture identities and references inside the same SQL transaction before any ownership publication, raising a database error on incompatible existing rows. Keep idempotent compatible inserts, and make the postcondition part of that transaction rather than a post-COMMIT Python assertion. Do not add another fixture framework.
findings.verification: Prepopulate the fixed user ID with another mailbox (and separately collide organization/project IDs), snapshot rows, run seed and require failure with the snapshot unchanged. Verify two normal runs preserve the exact intended users, tenant memberships and projects, including unrelated existing data.
findings.validation_status: Source-traced transaction ordering; no database mutation performed.

findings.title: Documented lint/format entry points bypass the no-implicit-toolchain-install preflight
findings.evidence: dev.py, verify.py and dependencies.py invoke preflight.check(), but the separately documented lint.py check/fmt commands do not. lint.py invokes cargo fmt/metadata/clippy directly, allowing rustup to auto-install a missing pinned toolchain. just migrate/openapi and lint-controls similarly call Cargo without the guard. README promises scripts refuse absent Rust rather than install implicitly.
findings.consequence: A contributor following the standalone documented formatting/lint workflow can trigger the exact implicit host change that preflight was introduced to prevent. The guarantee depends on which entry point happened to invoke the same tooling.
findings.remedy: Make the Rust-only prerequisite check a reusable narrow function called by every Cargo-running entry point (or one canonical guarded Cargo runner). Separate it from service prerequisites so formatting does not unnecessarily require Podman/OpenSSL. If toolchain auto-install is now desired, explicitly change the policy/docs instead of retaining a false guarantee.
findings.verification: Using an isolated fake executable boundary, expose rustup with the required toolchain absent and a cargo sentinel. Every documented Rust command must fail before invoking cargo; with the toolchain present, ordinary commands must retain behavior. No real toolchain installation is needed for this regression.
findings.validation_status: Static call-path inspection; no tools installed or commands under review executed.

findings.title: Architecture fitness silently exempts every newly added workspace crate
findings.evidence: violations() continues for any package name not in the hard-coded LAYERS map, and internal dependency restrictions only apply when the target is also in that map. Adding a new workspace adapter/helper therefore both exempts its own dependencies and lets domain/application depend on it regardless of its infrastructure dependencies. The gate uses --no-deps and has no unclassified-workspace-member check. Negative controls mutate only existing known crate names.
findings.consequence: The architectural guard fails open precisely when the template grows: an accidental indirect domain-to-infrastructure edge through a new crate passes while the check still announces dependency direction enforcement. This is a guard defect, not evidence that the current eight-crate graph violates layering.
findings.remedy: Require every workspace member to have an explicit layer classification and fail on unknown internal targets; validate all workspace edges under that classification. Keep a small closed policy rather than building a generic architecture framework. Do not promise SQL-in-controller or authorization-bypass detection from Cargo edges alone.
findings.verification: Add negative controls with a new workspace crate, a domain-to-new-adapter-to-SQLx edge and a renamed package; all must fail until a valid explicit classification is supplied. Preserve existing permitted dev dependencies and production graph checks.
findings.validation_status: Source-traced fail-open branches; no architecture suite executed.

observations.assessment: All 104 assigned docs/evidence paths were assessed as historical logs, manifests or claims, not current executable source. RED and negative-control failures are intentional. The archived library spike supports the stated stock-store and CSRF boundary observations, not a blanket security or incompatibility claim. Its lockfile/source remain evidence fixtures, not another production workspace.

At frozen revision results.json has 25 gates, all zero exit; rust-tests.log sums to 39 passing results. The independent fresh-checkout report names e966e69c7be4b3fa9011a287b3a8111e4b80b63d, not the reviewed HEAD. Current README/acceptance still call independent acceptance pending while that historical report records completion for its specific revision; reconcile status by revision, do not silently reuse it for future changes.

Pinned image digests and dependency locks, loopback fixture ports, nonroot/read-only OCI execution, separate migration credential/runtime role, workspace lint inheritance, narrowly versioned cargo-deny exceptions and generated-file exclusions are explicit. No project license was invented. Deployment Compose is accurately labeled unexecuted; image scanning, hosting CI and production deployment are not asserted.

The highest-value simplification is one explicit container/process lifecycle owner shared by dependency/dev/verify/compatibility paths, with canonical fixture settings. Compose and Python currently duplicate image/port definitions and have documented behavioral differences (TLS and Redis defaults). Avoid a generic orchestration framework; centralize only actual repeated ownership and failure semantics.
